tytul: Concord grape jelly with powdered pectin (NCHFP)
wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for grape jelly made from Concord grape juice with powdered pectin. [T:SLO-172]

akapity: NCHFP uses 5 cups of grape juice (about 3.5 pounds of Concord grapes and 1 cup of water), 1 package of powdered pectin and 7 cups of sugar, which makes about 8 or 9 half-pint jars. [T:SLO-172]
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml. [T:ACI-195]
NCHFP warns not to reduce the sugar in traditional recipes: too little sugar prevents gelling and may allow yeasts and molds to grow. [T:SLO-001]
Sterilize the jars and prepare two-piece lids according to the manufacturer's directions. [T:SLO-173]

NCHFP puts the empty jars right side up on the rack in a boiling-water canner and fills the canner and jars with hot (not boiling) water to 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the tops of the jars. [T:SLO-120]
To sterilize empty jars, NCHFP boils them for 10 minutes below 1000 ft, and above that 1 minute longer for each additional thousand feet. [T:SLO-118]
JarAtlas rule for metres: boil the jars for 10 minutes up to 300 m, and add 1 minute for every further 300 m or part of it. [T:SLO-119]
Sort and wash fully ripe grapes and remove the stems. [T:SLO-173]
Crush the grapes, add the water, cover and bring to a boil over high heat. [T:SLO-173]
Reduce the heat, simmer for 10 minutes and extract the juice. [T:SLO-173]
To keep tartrate crystals from forming in the jelly, let the juice stand overnight in a cool place, then strain it through two layers of damp cheesecloth to remove the crystals. [T:SLO-174]
Mix the measured juice with the pectin and, stirring constantly over high heat, bring it quickly to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. [T:SLO-175]
Add the sugar, keep stirring, bring back to a full rolling boil and boil hard for 1 minute. [T:SLO-175]
Remove from the heat and skim off the foam quickly. [T:SLO-175]
Just before filling, remove and drain the hot sterilized jars one at a time. [T:SLO-120]
Fill the hot jelly immediately into hot, sterile jars, leaving 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of headspace. [T:SLO-176]
Wipe the jar rims with a damp clean paper towel, put on two-piece metal lids and process in a boiling-water canner. [T:SLO-176]
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars for 5 minutes. [T:SLO-177,ACI-176]
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased. [T:ACI-015]
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process them for 10 minutes. [T:SLO-178,ACI-176]
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 15 minutes. [T:SLO-179,ACI-176]
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m. [T:ACI-176]
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage. [T:ACI-015]
The NCHFP table gives times only for half-pint and pint jars. [T:SLO-177]
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml. [T:ACI-179,ACI-174]
Keep opened jelly in the refrigerator at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or lower. [T:SLO-018]
Regular full-sugar cooked jellies like this one are best kept in the refrigerator for 1 month after opening. [T:SLO-018]
Discard jelly with mold on it; USDA and microbiologists advise against scooping out the mold and eating the rest. [T:SLO-012]
